description: Equipo hecho para divertirse y pasarla chill.
summary:
MOON AIM is an interactive web tool that helps mission planners, educators and the public evaluate where and when to land near the lunar south pole. On a polar map (70°S–90°S), users pick one of eight candidate sites or enter coordinates, set the UTC date and time, and adjust their lander's limits. The tool returns a Landing Safety Index (LSI, 0 to 100), solar illumination, Earth visibility for direct communication, and a plain-language explanation in English and Spanish.
To do this, MOON AIM queries JPL Horizons ephemerides for the Sun and Earth positions on the chosen date, and falls back to a local model if the service is unavailable. From the Clementine lunar mosaic it estimates slope and roughness for each cell, and combines them with illumination and Earth visibility to color a viability layer: green, amber or red. It also searches for optimal zones and proposes a divert within the Δv budget when the selected point is risky.
details:
0. The problem

Missions to the lunar south pole face extreme lighting and communication constraints: the Sun stays near the horizon, terrain casts long shadows, and Earth sits low in the sky. Planning takes careful coordination between science and engineering teams. Tools to determine Sun and Earth positions at candidate sites exist, but their complicated interfaces make it hard to evaluate critical information efficiently. An intuitive tool is needed so mission planners, educators and the public can compare sites and dates quickly.

1. What we built / What it is

MOON AIM is a single-page web application (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) that draws an interactive polar map of the lunar south pole and evaluates any point on it for a chosen mission date and time. It includes:

  • A base map (Clementine mosaic, 70°S–90°S) with 1x to 18x zoom and a viability overlay with adjustable opacity.
  • Eight candidate sites: Shackleton Rim, Connecting Ridge, Faustini Rim A, Haworth Massif, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1 and Schrödinger Basin.
  • Custom coordinate entry and UTC date and time selection.
  • Lander parameters: maximum slope, nozzle clearance, minimum solar illumination, minimum Earth visibility and divert budget (Δv).
  • Point telemetry: slope, roughness, solar illumination, Earth visibility, surface temperature and tip-over safety factor.

2. How it works

  1. Ephemeris: when the date or time changes, the app responds immediately with a local analytical model and queries JPL Horizons for the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth. If the query succeeds, the badge reads "JPL Horizons"; if not, the tool keeps working on the local model.
  2. Terrain: the brightness and gradient of the Clementine mosaic are converted into an estimate of slope and roughness (rocks) for each cell.
  3. Light and communication: solar illumination and Earth visibility are estimated by combining terrain, Sun direction and Earth libration for the chosen date.
  4. LSI: each point receives a score from 0 to 100 that penalizes excess slope, rocks versus nozzle clearance, lack of sunlight and lack of Earth visibility. It is shown in three ranges: optimal (75 or more), marginal (45 to 74) and hazardous (below 45).
  5. Search and divert: the "Find Optimal Zones" button shows a sample of five high-LSI zones, and a diagnostic log proposes an alternate trajectory within the radius allowed by the Δv budget.

3. How to use it / Uses / Who it is for

How to use it: choose a candidate site, click the map or type coordinates; set the UTC date and time; adjust your lander's limits; read the LSI, telemetry and plain-language explanation, then change the date to see how the result varies.

Who it is for:

  • Mission planners: compare sites, dates and lander margins quickly.
  • Educators and students: understand why place and timing matter, with clear explanations in English and Spanish.
  • The public: explore the lunar south pole visually and interactively.

4. What makes it different / Features

  • It brings terrain, solar illumination and Earth visibility into one screen instead of separate tools.
  • A single, easy-to-read index (LSI) with colors and a plain-language explanation.
  • Adjustable lander limits, so the same map serves different vehicles.
  • It uses NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data and keeps a local model as backup.
  • Bilingual interface (English and Spanish) and a map that zooms up to 18x.
  • It searches for optimal zones and suggests a safe divert within the Δv budget.

5. Impact / Innovation

Impact: it shortens the time needed to evaluate sites and dates, makes the balance between power, communication and safety visible, and brings lunar exploration closer to students and the public.

Innovation: it integrates terrain, illumination and Earth link into a single index that changes with the mission date and time, combines real JPL Horizons data with a local fallback, and presents the result in accessible language.

Next steps: replace the terrain estimate with LOLA elevation data, compute each site's true horizon, show time remaining before sunset and Earthset, and add a timeline and side-by-side site comparison.
